findings.message: The in-pod watchdog starts its FLEET_AGENT_TIMEOUT clock when the agent starts, not when the container starts. `activeDeadlineSeconds` (`lib/manifest.sh:15`) counts from Job start and is only 600 s longer. Pre-agent time comes off that 600 s margin: the egress wait (up to 60 s), clone, `fetch_claude` (its binary curl alone allows `-m 900`), and branch resume. If those steps take more than 10 minutes, the Job controller kills the pod before the watchdog fires. The writeback container is the pod's main container and has not started yet, so it never runs. This contradicts the README's deadline guarantee (`README.md:89`). Fix: record a start timestamp at the top of the entrypoint, give the watchdog the remaining budget (`FLEET_AGENT_TIMEOUT - elapsed`), and fail early when no budget is left.
findings.scenario: Codex dispatch with FLEET_DEADLINE_MINUTES=120 on a large repo whose clone through the proxy takes 11 min. The watchdog would fire at 131 min, but activeDeadlineSeconds kills the pod at 130 min. The writeback container never starts, so the refreshed auth.json (the refresh token was already rotated) is never written to the vault. The vault keeps a consumed token, and the assignee's next codex run fails auth.

findings.message: The lookalike fix only rejects branches whose last segment differs (`specclaw/1049-x`). Any remote branch ending in `/<change>` under any prefix still matches, and the first one is resumed. Match the configured branch prefix (`git.branch_prefix` / the `branch` recorded in state.json) instead of a bare suffix.
findings.scenario: The remote has `refs/heads/users/bob/049-x` (a personal experiment) and no `specclaw/049-x`. ls-remote matches `refs/heads/*049-x`, and awk accepts the suffix `/049-x`. The pod checks out bob's branch and builds on top of it. At delivery, state.branch (`specclaw/049-x`) differs from HEAD, so nothing is pushed. The run is recorded as failed and the agent's work is lost.

findings.message: The R11 fix ("could not ask is skip, never missing") was applied to every kube check except `check_context`. A transient network or auth error on `kubectl version` is reported as `missing context` and counted as needing attention. Only treat a missing or unknown kube context as `missing`. When the server could not be reached, print `skip context: could not ask the cluster: <err>` and return 2. Add a KUBE_FLAKY row that also fails `version`.
findings.scenario: The context exists, but the API server answers `Unable to connect to the server: i/o timeout`. Doctor prints `missing context: cannot reach the cluster` and exits 1 ('need attention'). Every other kube check in the same run prints `skip …`.

findings.message: On GNU coreutils (the ubuntu CI runner), `stat -f '%Lp' file` treats `-f` as file-system mode and `%Lp` as a second file operand. It prints the file-system block for the real file and exits 1. The `|| stat -c '%a'` fallback then appends `600`, so `token_file` holds multiple lines and `nested_auth` fails in CI. Detect the platform, or use `stat -c '%a' f 2>/dev/null || stat -f '%Lp' f`, so the GNU form runs first.

`trigger_pushed_tree` passes FLEET_REMOTE and FLEET_REF to `git fetch` before `parse_dispatch_args` validates the ref. A value starting with `-` is parsed as a git option. Validate the ref with the same branch-name rule before the fetch, or put `--` before the positional arguments.

Tag splitting, trimming and case-folding is written four times: bash `has_auto_tag`, bash `already_handled` (`lib/workitem.sh`), jq `auto` in `auto_tagged_by`, and Python `PY_TAGS` in specclaw-azdo-issue. Each uses a different whitespace and lower-casing definition. Today they agree for ASCII tags. Consider one shared helper so they cannot drift.

The settings list omits `FLEET_CLAUDE_VERSION`, which `parse_pod_inputs` requires for claude jobs. It also omits `FLEET_IMAGE_PULL_SECRET`, `FLEET_NODE_LABEL` and `FLEET_KUBE_CONTEXT`, which the README documents. Add them so the skill matches the code.
